dialogue_quality_notes: Participants clearly identify linked but distinct problems: schedule, smell, and cleanliness (e.g., C: "The pan, the smell, the schedule.").
Several speakers give concrete constraints (D: work arrival time; A: can't eat that late), which grounds the negotiation.
C advances a specific behavioral proposal (clean your own things immediately), but others do not accept it within the transcript.
evaluation.final_reason: By the end of round 8 multiple substantive incompatibilities remain. The core scheduling dispute between D (needs ~8:15–8:30) and A (cannot wait that late) was stated repeatedly and not resolved. The smell/ventilation complaint (B) and the dirty pan/blame issue (C) were discussed and C proposed a cleaning norm, but no one explicitly accepted that rule or agreed to change behavior. Key lines: D: "I usually get back around 8... around 8:15 or 8:30?" A: "That's quite late for me to eat." and C: "What if we just agree to clean our own things as soon as we're done?" — proposal not adopted by others, so no settlement.
position_change_notes: A consistently maintained that they cook immediately after work and cannot wait until 8:30 (no softening).
D consistently maintained an earlier-late-home constraint and requested a schedule (no softening).
C moved from calling out the unwashed pan to proposing a concrete behavioral rule (clean your own things immediately).
B stayed focused on the smell and its practical impact (sleep), not on proposing scheduling solutions.

round_scores.evidence: D: "Every night it's the same... When it's finally free, it's too late for me to start cooking a proper meal." A: "So what time do you want to use it?" — scheduling disagreement introduced.
D: "I usually get back around 8. So, maybe around 8:15 or 8:30?" A: "That's quite late for me to eat." — clear disagreement about acceptable cooking time.

B: "The smell goes everywhere. Can you just use the fan and open the window?" A: "I do use the fan. And I open the window." — a separate smell/ventilation complaint arises while schedule dispute remains unresolved.

B: "Well it's not working. The whole flat smells." C: "Never mind the smell for a minute. Who left the pan in the sink from last night?" — responsibility for unwashed pan added to ongoing smell and scheduling issues.

D: "Can we please sort out a schedule for the stove first? That's a problem every single night." A: "I cook when I finish work. I can't just wait until 8:30." — direct, opposing constraints; stronger scheduling conflict.
D: "I can't get home any earlier. So what am I supposed to do? I have to eat too." A: "I don't know. We all have to eat." — positions restated without movement toward resolution.

B: "Forget the schedule. What are we going to do about the smell? I need to sleep." C: "The pan, the smell, the schedule. It's all the same problem. None of us are cleaning up properly." — conflict broadens to cleanliness norms and links multiple issues.

D: "Cleaning is one thing. The schedule is another. We can wash the pan, but I still won't have time to cook." C: "If the kitchen is clean when it's your turn, that saves you time, doesn't it? What if we just agree to clean our own things as soon as we're done?" — cleaning moves toward a concrete proposal while scheduling remains unresolved.

substantive_insights: The scheduling conflict arises from incompatible work/end-of-day times rather than mere preference, making simple rescheduling difficult.
Smell complaints are tied partly to cleanliness (unwashed pan) and partly to ventilation effectiveness; fixing cleanliness may reduce but not eliminate the smell problem.
Absent shared norms, small failures (leaving a pan) cascade into broader grievances about fairness and convenience.
Participants prioritize different issues: D emphasizes schedule, B emphasizes sleep/odor, C links cleanliness to both, A emphasizes personal routine.
